ch.n: How to Read a Single Candle
ch.str: How to Read a Single Candle

ch.n: A candlestick is the densest piece of in
ch.str: A candlestick is the densest piece of information in finance. In one shape, you can see a day's worth of price action — where it opened, where it closed, the highest and lowest points it touched, and whether buyers or sellers won. Once you can read one candle, you can read a chart.

ch.n: The shape of a candle reflects what happ
ch.str: The shape of a candle reflects what happened during the period. A long body means a strong, decisive move. Long wicks mean the price went somewhere — but came back. The combination tells you who was in control and who got rejected. Here are four candles every trader recognises:

ch.n: A single candle is one data point — cont
ch.str: A single candle is one data point — context matters more than the shape. A hammer at the top of an uptrend means almost nothing. A hammer after a long downtrend, near a support level, on high volume — that's worth paying attention to. Candles by themselves are noise. Candles in context are signal.

ch.n: The Two Most Useful Concepts in TA
ch.str: The Two Most Useful Concepts in TA

ch.n: If you only ever learn two things from t
ch.str: If you only ever learn two things from technical analysis, learn these. Trends tell you which direction the market is moving. Support and resistance tell you where it's likely to pause, bounce, or break. Together, they're the entire foundation of price-based trading.

ch.n: A market is always in one of three state
ch.str: A market is always in one of three states. Sounds obvious — but most retail mistakes come from trading against the trend, or pretending one exists when the market is actually flat.

ch.n: Price oscillates between a ceiling and a
ch.str: Price oscillates between a ceiling and a floor. Neither side is winning. Most markets are sideways most of the time.

ch.n: Price has memory. When a stock has bounc
ch.str: Price has memory. When a stock has bounced off the same level three times, traders watching the chart remember — and they place orders there next time. That collective memory creates the level. Self-fulfilling, but real.

ch.n: PRICE BOUNCES OFF SUPPORT (FLOOR) AND RE
ch.str: PRICE BOUNCES OFF SUPPORT (FLOOR) AND RESISTANCE (CEILING) MULTIPLE TIMES

ch.n: A price level where buyers historically
ch.str: A price level where buyers historically step in. The more times price bounces off it, the stronger it gets. When support breaks, it often becomes the new resistance — what was a floor becomes a ceiling.

ch.n: A price level where sellers historically
ch.str: A price level where sellers historically step in. Often round numbers (50 EGP, 100 EGP) or recent highs. When resistance breaks, it often becomes the new support — old ceiling becomes the new floor.

ch.n: The Three Indicators Every Trader Knows
ch.str: The Three Indicators Every Trader Knows

Indicators are mathematical formulas applied to price to highlight things the eye might miss. There are hundreds. Most are variations on each other. These three — Moving Averages, RSI, and MACD — cover 80% of what retail traders actually use. Important caveat upfront: indicators lag the market. They tell you what already happened, not what will happen.

ch.n: The average closing price over the last
ch.str: The average closing price over the last N days. Smooths out daily noise to reveal the underlying trend. The two most-watched: 50-day MA (medium-term trend) and 200-day MA (long-term trend).

ch.n: A 0–100 score that asks: has this stock
ch.str: A 0–100 score that asks: has this stock been gaining or losing recently, and how aggressively? Above 70 means "overbought" — the rally may be exhausted. Below 30 means "oversold" — the selling may have gone too far.

ch.n: RSI is most useful at extremes. A stock
ch.str: RSI is most useful at extremes. A stock at RSI 75 in a strong uptrend can stay overbought for weeks — selling on RSI alone is a common rookie mistake.

ch.n: A momentum indicator. It compares two mo
ch.str: A momentum indicator. It compares two moving averages (typically 12-day and 26-day) and shows whether they're converging or diverging. When the lines cross, it's a signal that momentum is shifting.

ch.n: New traders often add 8 indicators to a
ch.str: New traders often add 8 indicators to a single chart, hoping more is better. It's not — they're mostly measuring the same thing. Pick two or three, learn what they actually mean, and trust the chart's price action above any indicator. Indicators don't predict — they describe.

ch.n: Certain chart shapes appear so often tha
ch.str: Certain chart shapes appear so often that they have names and reputations. Some traders swear by them. Others think they're glorified pareidolia — finding faces in clouds. The truth is probably in between: patterns work partly because they capture real market psychology, and partly because enough people watch them that they become self-fulfilling.

ch.n: A sharp rally followed by a small downwa
ch.str: A sharp rally followed by a small downward channel — like a flag on a flagpole. Usually a continuation pattern: the trend resumes after a brief pause.

ch.n: The human eye is built to find patterns
ch.str: The human eye is built to find patterns — even where none exist. Once you learn what a head-and-shoulders looks like, you'll see them everywhere. The real test is statistical: do these patterns produce reliable returns out-of-sample, after costs? Academic studies are mixed at best. Treat patterns as one piece of evidence, not as predictions.

ch.n: What Charts Can and Can't Tell You
ch.str: What Charts Can and Can't Tell You

Technical analysis has fierce believers and fierce skeptics — both with valid points. The honest position is that TA is a useful lens for some things and useless for others. Understanding the line between them is what separates a thoughtful trader from a chart-worshipper.

ch.n: TA isn't magic. When it works, it works
ch.str: TA isn't magic. When it works, it works for two reasons. First — self-fulfilling prophecy. If enough traders watch the 200-day moving average, they'll buy when price approaches it from above. That collective behaviour is what makes the level "support." Second — behavioural patterns. Markets are made of humans, and humans react predictably to the same emotional triggers. Fear at the bottom, greed at the top. Charts capture the footprint of those reactions. When TA fails, it's usually because something exogenous (news, regulation, macro shock) overwhelms the patterns. The patterns don't disappear — they just stop dominating.

ch.n: TA is a lens, not a crystal ball. The be
ch.str: TA is a lens, not a crystal ball. The best traders use it alongside fundamentals (the lens we cover in Session 5), risk management, and humility about what they don't know. A chart pattern by itself is not a reason to trade. A chart pattern plus a thesis, a defined risk, and the willingness to be wrong — that's a setup. The next session covers the other half of the equation: how to read the company behind the ticker.
